senses.definition: the official group of people whose job is to make sure that people obey the law, to prevent crime, and to catch criminals

examples.text: The police are looking for two men who were seen near the store.
Someone reported the missing car to the police.
Police were called to the house late last night.
examples.note: without the, as in news reports

compare.note: cop is the informal word for one police officer
a police officer is one member of the police

word_family.note: to keep order in a place

usage_note: Police is a singular form used with a plural verb: the police are here, the police have arrived. It has no plural of its own and no singular for one person: say a police officer (or, less often now, a policeman or policewoman), never a police. In news reports the word often appears without the: Police were called to the scene.

learner_errors.incorrect: A police stopped me on the road.
learner_errors.correct: A police officer stopped me on the road.
learner_errors.note: Police is the whole group; for one person say a police officer.

adaptation.semantic: One word for the organization and for its officers together; for one officer English needs police officer. Many languages have a single countable word for an officer and a different word for the force; keep the two apart.
adaptation.grammar: Police is plural in grammar though singular in form: the police are, not the police is. No article a: a police officer, not a police. It has no plural. Learners of many backgrounds make both mistakes.
adaptation.culture: In many English-speaking countries the police are organized locally, by city or region, so a police department or a police force is a local body. The emergency telephone number differs from country to country. Cop is the common informal word for an officer.
adaptation.false_friends: In some languages a look-alike word means an insurance document. English police is only the law-keeping organization; an insurance document is a policy.
adaptation.pronunciation: Stress on the second syllable, with a weak first vowel and a long ee: puh-LEESS. Learners often stress the first syllable; keep the stress on the second. The final sound is s, not z.
